---
title: "Language"
subtitle: "Entities, activities and their organization, written down to be run"
---

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
A mechanism is *entities and activities organized such that they are productive of regular
changes from start or set-up to finish or termination conditions* (Machamer, Darden & Craver,
2000, p. 3). Plexus is a language for
writing a mechanism down in exactly those terms — the entities with their states and
relations, the activities that act on them, and their organization in space, in time and
across levels — so that the description can be run, fitted to observations, and shown
to be missing an activity. Every activity is an *operator*: it names the entities
it acts on, the state it needs, the relations between those entities, and one or more
numerical implementations. The research programme has three objectives. First, an algebra of
activities. Second, to decompose the existing corpus of simulation models into that
language. Third, to build differentiable implementations of every operator, so that
mechanistic models can be inferred from biological data.
:::

## Introduction

Computational biology has produced a rich ecosystem of simulation frameworks. Neural
simulators model electrical activity, reaction–diffusion systems model chemical transport,
particle and continuum methods model mechanics, while vertex, Cellular Potts and
active-matter models describe multicellular tissues. These frameworks remain largely
incompatible. Combining electrical signalling, mechanics, metabolism and development
requires coupling several specialized simulators whose underlying abstractions differ
fundamentally, and each simulator carries its own representation of what a mechanism is,
so that models are hard to compare, compose and extend. This fragmentation is not primarily
a numerical problem. It is a language problem.

Biology already has an account of what a mechanism is, even if it is rarely written out.
In the account of Machamer, Darden and Craver, a mechanism has two halves. *Entities* are
the things: they have properties and stand in spatial relations to one another. *Activities*
are what the things do: they are the producers of change. And the two are *organized* —
spatially, by location, shape and contact; temporally, by order, rate and duration; and
hierarchically, because what the parts do at one level constitutes what the whole does at
the next. A mechanism starts from set-up conditions and ends at termination conditions, and
the description bottoms out in activities that the field takes as fundamental. This is the
account a cell biologist uses tacitly whenever a paper ends with a summary cartoon: named
parts, arrows between them, boxes inside boxes. The paper also gives that cartoon its two
names. A *mechanism schema* is an abstract description whose placeholders can be filled
with known parts and activities; a *mechanism sketch* is one with gaps — black boxes that
no known activity yet fills. A complete description exhibits *productive continuity without
gaps* from set-up to termination conditions, and the continuity lies in the arrows.

Plexus takes that account literally. Instead of treating simulation frameworks as
fundamental, it treats entities and activities as the primary objects. An activity —
adhesion, diffusion, division, chemotaxis, electrical propagation, active stress — is
written as an *operator*, independently of how it is computed. The two words mean the same
thing in two dialects, and this page uses both. In this perspective biological modelling
becomes analogous to compiler design: just as a compiler separates a programming language
from its implementations through an intermediate representation, Plexus separates the
mechanism from its numerical realization.

Entities are heterogeneous — receptors, signalling proteins, cells, extracellular matrices,
tissues, fields — and they are organized across levels. Plexus makes this organization
explicit: each level carries its own entities and states, operators act between entities
within a level, and **aggregate ↑** and **broadcast ↓** connect the levels by carrying
state from parts to whole and from whole to parts. Decomposition therefore does not
flatten a tissue into one collection of variables. It keeps the organization through which
a mechanism at one level is composed with a mechanism at another.

The purpose of the decomposition is recomposition: to build complete mechanistic models
from reusable entities and activities. Making such compositions executable requires a
strong structural choice, and Plexus makes it by separating the language that states the
hypothesis from the code that runs it. The language declares entities, states, relations,
organization and activities; the interpreter resolves the declaration into numerical
implementations and runs them in the declared order. What the language guarantees is that
a hypothesis is well formed and complete. Whether it is *productive of* the change observed
is what running it establishes.

## The language

Plexus is built around four kinds of object. Two describe what exists — **sets** and their
**states**, together with the **fields** that make up the microenvironment — and one
describes what happens — the **operators**. A model is a composition of operators acting on
discrete and continuous biological objects, not a simulator-specific algorithm.

### Sets — the entities

A set is a collection of entities of one kind at one level of organization: genes,
proteins, cells, neurons, synapses, tissues, organs, organisms. Sets organize into
hierarchies that reflect biological organization — genes regulate proteins, proteins
determine what a cell does, cells assemble into tissues, tissues into organs — and each
level is represented uniformly as a set, so that the same language describes intracellular
signalling, multicellular mechanics, development and organ physiology. A set need not be
a whole organism's worth of one thing: the vertices of a cell sheet are a set, the
material points of a gel are a set, and both can be parts of the same cell.

### States — the properties

Every entity carries a state describing its current condition. Sets say *what exists*;
states say *what each entity carries*. The state schema is specific to each set. A protein
may carry a position, a binding state and the load it bears; a material point a position,
a velocity and a deformation gradient; a neuron a membrane voltage and a calcium level; a
cell a polarity, a stiffness and its gene-expression levels; a synapse a conductance and a
plastic weight. Operators transform states: they read selected state variables and write
updates to others, while the entities themselves remain what they were.

### Fields — the microenvironment

A field is a continuous quantity defined over space rather than over entities: a morphogen
concentration, a pressure, an extracellular signal, an electric potential, a matrix
density. Fields complement sets. Sets describe the discrete entities, fields the
continuous environment those entities live in, and operators couple the two through
explicit maps from entities to positions in space.

### Operators — the activities

An operator is one activity, and it is the fundamental object of the language. It
represents a single mechanism — adhesion, chemotaxis, diffusion, electrical propagation,
active stress, metabolism, growth, division — by a typed signature and one or more
numerical implementations. The signature states *what* change the activity produces; the
implementations state *how* it is computed. The signature declares

- the sets the activity acts on,
- the sets it changes,
- the state variables it reads and the ones it writes,
- the maps relating the participating sets.

The maps are the relations the mechanism needs. They say which protein belongs to which
cell, which synapses connect which neurons, or how cells relate to a field. Because the
relations are part of the signature, an operator is a typed morphism between sets, and the
spatial organization of the mechanism is declared with the activity rather than assumed by
the code.

## The operator algebra

The central hypothesis of Plexus is that a large fraction of the activities in the
simulation literature can be composed from a small number of elementary kinds. Rather
than introducing a new operator for every phenomenon, Plexus identifies a compact algebra
that is reused across mechanics, signalling, metabolism, development and physiology. There
are **eight** kinds, and here each is named first in a biologist's words:

- **lateral** — what neighbours do to each other within one set.
- **aggregate ↑** — integration: a whole reading its parts.
- **broadcast ↓** — top-down control: a whole imposing on its parts.
- **exchange** — traffic between entities and their microenvironment.
- **field** — the microenvironment's own life: diffusion, decay, reaction.
- **rewire** — remodelling: the relations change, the entities do not.
- **structural** — turnover: **divide** and **die**.
- **seed** — the set-up conditions, written once and never again.

The first five kinds change state and leave the organization intact. Rewire changes the
relations, structural changes the entities themselves, and seed writes what the others go
on to evolve. Together they are the elementary vocabulary of Plexus, and the
implementation recognizes exactly these eight.

![](figures/fig_ops.png){width=100% fig-align="center"}

**Lateral.** What entities of one set do to one another: mechanical forces between
proteins, adhesion and tension between neighbouring cells, juxtacrine signalling, contact
inhibition, gap-junction coupling, synaptic transmission, the reactions of a metabolic
network.

**Aggregate.** Integration. A whole reads its parts: a cell's shape from its vertices, a
cell's properties from its proteins, a neuron's input as the sum of its synaptic currents,
a tissue's shape as the collective consequence of its cells. This is the upward direction of
causation, the one usually called emergence.

**Broadcast.** Top-down control. A whole imposes on its parts: a cell's polarity on its
cytoskeleton, a material property on every point the cell owns, a fate decision on
everything the cell contains, a constraint the tissue places on its cells. Aggregate and
broadcast together are the upward and downward flow across levels of organization.

**Exchange.** A cell's traffic with its microenvironment: secretion, uptake, sensing,
transport, and mechanical load carried to and from the matrix — in numerical terms the
transfer between entities and a grid.

**Field.** The microenvironment's own dynamics — diffusion, decay, extracellular reaction
— mapping a field to itself without touching any set.

**Rewire.** Remodelling. Neighbour exchange in an epithelium, junction turnover, synaptic
plasticity, matrix remodelling: the relations between entities change, the entities do not,
and which entities take part in the next activity changes with them.

**Structural.** Turnover. A living tissue continuously changes its own composition:
**divide** creates entities and **die** removes them — proliferation, apoptosis,
extrusion. These operators change the organization itself, not only its state, and they
are what makes a tissue different from any inert material.

**Seed.** The set-up conditions: the egg, the pre-pattern, the segmentation a model starts
from. A seed writes a set's initial state once. It is confined to the first frame, so that
a starting condition cannot silently become a boundary condition applied at every step.

## Organization in time

A model is written as an ordered list of activities, the *schedule*, which says both in
what order and how often each runs. Formally, one step is the composition

$$\Phi = \mathcal{O}_n \circ \cdots \circ \mathcal{O}_1,$$

of the operators, whose repeated application generates the dynamics

$$x_{t+1} = \Phi(x_t),$$

where $x$ is the whole state — every set and every field at once. The schedule is the
temporal organization of the mechanism: its order, rate and duration. Activities run at
their own tempo — mechanics every step, diffusion, growth or division less often — so a
model is a multi-rate composition of mechanisms rather than one monolithic solver.

Operators are pure. None modifies state directly; each returns its contribution to the
change. If operator $\mathcal{O}_i$ produces the increment $\Delta_i$, the complete update
is

$$\Delta = \sum_i \Delta_i,$$

before it is passed to the numerical implementation. Two things follow. Activities stay
independent and composable: adding a mechanism is adding an operator to the schedule.
And the language stays independent of its numerical realization: the schedule states the
hypothesis, the implementation states how it is evaluated.

## Organization across levels

A cell is a compartment, and a compartment holds parts of different kinds. A set may be
contained in another — proteins in a cell, cells in a tissue, tissues in an organism —
through an explicit part → whole map, and one whole may contain several distinct sets: the
same cell can hold receptors, signalling proteins, cytoskeletal elements and material
points. These sets remain distinct, with their own state and their own activities, while
sharing the same parent. A vertex model that treats a cell as a polygon and a
reaction–diffusion model that treats it as a well-mixed bag are each a caricature; here the
same cell is both at once, because both are sets under one parent. Each level also runs at
its own tempo, and no level is reduced to a parameter of the one above it.

![](figures/fig_hier.png){width=70% fig-align="center"}

Activities run within a level or across it. Within a cell, operators couple receptors →
signalling proteins → cytoskeleton. Across the part → whole map, **aggregate ↑** builds
the whole's state from its parts — a cell's position from its material points, a neuron's
input from its synapses — and **broadcast ↓** carries the whole's state to its parts — a
material property to every point a cell owns, a constraint imposed by the tissue. Causation
runs both ways, and both directions are operators like any other.

Fields belong to levels too. **Exchange** couples a set to the field at its own level, so
that a protein concentration inside the cell, a morphogen among cells and a mechanical grid
under the tissue coexist as distinct objects.

Proteins → cells → tissues is therefore not a pipeline of separate simulators. It is one
compositional graph: several sets inside each whole, operators joining them locally,
aggregate and broadcast joining the levels. The same eight kinds serve throughout, and
another level of organization needs no new machinery.

## Bottoming out: numerical implementations

Every mechanistic description stops somewhere: it bottoms out in activities the field is
content to take as given. In Plexus that floor is the numerical implementation. The
operator algebra states the biological meaning of a model; every operator may admit
several implementations satisfying the same typed signature, which differ in how they
compute and not in what they mean. Choosing an implementation is a numerical decision,
never a biological one.

This accommodates a broad range of methods. A mechanical activity may be implemented with
the material point method, finite elements, a vertex model, a phase field, a Cellular Potts
model or an optimal-transport formulation. A signalling activity may use Hodgkin–Huxley
equations, a graph neural network or a neural ordinary differential equation. A field
activity may use finite differences, finite elements, a neural implicit representation or a
spectral method. These coexist in one language because they satisfy the same contracts.

Implementations may also integrate differently. Depending on the activity, an
implementation may advance first-order states such as concentrations or membrane voltages,
second-order states such as mechanical accelerations, and rely on explicit, implicit or
adaptive solvers. These choices affect cost and accuracy, not the biological reading of the
model.

The distinction changes how models are compared. Traditional frameworks compare complete
simulators, which entangle the mechanism with the numerics. Plexus separates the two
questions: hypotheses are compared through the activities they compose, numerical methods
through the implementations that realize those activities. There are then two independent
axes of progress. Biological innovation is discovering a new activity or a new
composition; numerical innovation is a faster or more accurate implementation of an
activity that already exists. Existing simulation frameworks become complementary backends
of one intermediate representation rather than competing paradigms.

## Mechanistic inverse modelling

A formal language of mechanisms exists first of all so that mechanisms can be identified
from observations. Rather than calibrating simulations by hand, the aim is to infer the
parameters, the spatial organization and the constitutive laws of a biological system from
imaging data.

Plexus makes this possible by giving every operator at least one differentiable
implementation satisfying its signature. Differentiability is then a property of the
language rather than of a particular simulator: whatever the backend, gradients propagate
through a composition of explicit activities rather than through monolithic code.

This changes what inverse modelling means. The traditional approach assumes the mechanism
is already right and searches for the parameter values that best reproduce the
observations. That works when the forward model is complete and misleads when an activity
is missing: tuning the parameters that exist improves the fit while merely compensating
for the activity that does not.

In Plexus, parameters stay attached to explicit activities rather than to an opaque model.
Mechanical properties belong to mechanical operators, reaction rates to biochemical ones,
conductances to signalling ones, and spatial fields to the activities that generate them,
so that estimation keeps the mechanistic reading of the model.

Residuals acquire the same reading. A persistent mismatch between simulation and
experiment no longer means only that the parameters are wrong; it may mean that the
present composition of activities cannot produce the observed change. In the paper's terms,
a residual that will not go away is the mark of a sketch: a black box where an activity
belongs. Differentiability therefore does more than make optimization efficient. It lets competing mechanistic
hypotheses be compared quantitatively while each keeps its explicit structure.

## Agentic mechanistic discovery

Writing mechanisms as explicit activities turns discovery from a parameter-optimization
problem into a language-exploration problem. Because activities are operators rather than
code buried in a simulator, they are directly accessible to an agent.

Plexus proposes a three-loop strategy, each loop at a different level of abstraction,
moving from existing models toward new biological knowledge.

**Loop I: Understanding.** The first loop reads an existing simulation model. Rather than
treating the simulator as opaque code, the agent decomposes it into Plexus operators,
names the activities it implements and the entities they act on, and reconstructs an
explicit mechanistic description. Existing frameworks become repositories of reusable
entities and activities.

**Loop II: Fitting.** The second loop estimates the parameters, spatial fields and set-up
conditions of the resulting mechanism by fitting it directly to experimental observations.
Because every operator has a differentiable implementation, optimization keeps an explicit
correspondence between parameters and activities.

**Loop III: Discovery.** The third loop reads the residual that remains after fitting.
A persistent discrepancy is taken as evidence that the composition is incomplete rather
than poorly parameterized. The agent proposes alternative activities, compares competing
mechanistic hypotheses, and extends the algebra whenever the activities it has cannot
produce the change observed — turning a sketch into a schema, one filled box at a time.

Together the three loops make simulation, inverse modelling and hypothesis generation
successive stages of one workflow. The language itself becomes the object of discovery:
new biological knowledge is a new activity, or a new composition of activities, and not
merely a new parameter value.
